public_comment.topic: Questioned why the Keing-Lancaster interconnection was ruled out by engineers, gave his own comparison of PFAS, iron and manganese levels and costs between well sources, and asked for a written explanation from the engineering firm.
Said the district should not spend money until state and federal PFAS rules and the 3M/DuPont litigation are settled, and that treatment plant costs quoted by contractors are far too high.

minutes.headline: Water commissioners approved a Rolling Acres tie-in purchase and reworked the PFAS survey after public pushback on treatment options.
minutes.summary: The Water District commissioners approved purchasing materials for a new water main tie-in feeding Rolling Acres and spent most of the meeting revising a public survey meant to gauge community priorities on PFAS treatment, hardness, redundancy and cost. In public comment, residents pressed the board on why combining the Lancaster and Keing well sources for treatment had been ruled out, questioned treatment plant costs, and argued residents should get more cost detail before any survey goes out; the board agreed to revise the draft and bring it back in two weeks.

what_happened.line: Commissioners voted to approve materials for a new water main tie-in feeding Rolling Acres, using HR Prescott as vendor.
After residents pushed back, the board agreed to revise its PFAS treatment survey and bring a new draft back in two weeks.
The board also agreed to ask its engineering firm for a written explanation of why treating the Lancaster and Keing wells together was not recommended.
Residents argued treatment plant costs are too high and said the district should wait for state and federal PFAS rules and related litigation to settle before spending further.

why_it_matters: The PFAS survey will shape which treatment path the district pursues for the Lancaster, Keing and Hickory Hills wells, which affects future water rates.
The Rolling Acres tie-in is a capital purchase drawn from the water fund, separate from the PFAS treatment decision.
Residents are asking for clearer cost comparisons before any survey or vote goes out, which could change the timeline or shape of the district's PFAS plan.
